SHOOTING AFFRAYS
AT ASH FORK
A shooting affray occurred at Ash Fork last Friday in which a Mexican named Francisco Basquez was shot five times by Enriques Barajos. The two men quarreled over the affections of a fair but fickle senorita, and so intense were they in their ardor for the winning of the senorita, that they both met on the woman's threshold at the same time, and the collision followed.

There was little ceremony after the two men met, and while in the room Barajos whipped out a 45 colts and emptied every shot into the body of Basquez. So close to the latter's body was the weapon, that his clothes were ignited. The blaze was extinguished by the
Basquez was at once taken to the hospital at Prescott, where he died Monday evening. At last accounts Barajos had not been captured.

Another shooting affray occurred Sunday evening at Ash Ferk, when a colored man used his six-shooter on a Mexican, but managed to make his escape into the foothills although the officers at once gave chase and fired a number of shots at the fleeing negro.
We were unable to learn the particulars leading up to the shooting. ____

charles-howard-frankfort-1910-08-28.A1:
MOB STORMS JAIL
TO LYNCH NEGRO
Crowd Disperses Just as Acting Governor Is Ready to Call Troops.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 28.—Frankfort jail was stormed just before daylight this morning by a mob of 200 men bent on lynching Charles Howard, a negro charged with the murder of Edward Rice.
While the mob was finally driven off without injury to any one, Acting Governor Cox was on the verge of ordering out troops when the crowd dispersed.
charles-howard-frankfort-1910-08-28.A4:
Three Deals in One Day. J. F. Ellis sold Saturday a handsome residence on South Main, a fine farm near Pembroke and a cottage on O'Neill avenue. List your property with the man who SELLS real estate. SAVED FROM LYNCHING By Mayor And Jailer Of Frankfort.
Frankfort, Ky., Aug. 30.—Charles Howard, a negro, who shot to death Edward Rice, a white man, owes his life to Jailer Lucas and Mayor Polsgrove. Howard, who claims he shot in self defense, was threatened with lynching by an angry mob around the jail, but before harm was done the jailer and mayor contrived to convey him safely to the jail at Lexington. Mayor Polsgrove is resolved to have no more lynchings in Frankfort.
charles-howard-frankfort-1910-08-28.A5:
Judge Stout After Mob Members.
At Frankfort Monday Judge R. L. Stout delivered a strong charge to the grand jury in reference to the attempt of a mob to take a negro from the jail there some days ago insisting that the grand jury investigate the matter thoroughly, without fear or favor, and bring the members of the mob to justice, if possible.

After delivering the usual charge as to ordinary infractions of the laws as to gambling, illegal whiskey selling and some minor matters he said in part:

"There is another matter I want to call your very earnest attention to. I have been informed that but for the fearless action of your county officials there would have been a murder committed by a mob right at the doors of this courthouse only a few days ago; that a large body of men handed themselves together and came to the jail and demanded possession of a prisoner who was already in the hands of the law. I want you to investigate this thoroughly.

"If citizens are to be allowed to take the administration of justice into their own hands and decide who shall be punished and who shall not, it will not be long till all private affairs and business matters will be controlled by such methods and anarchy will reign. That means there will be no law and no redress or any citizens. There is no bravery or courage in any man who joins with a lot o other men to kill a poor, cowering, trembling prisoner who is already in the custody of the law.
"I must insist that you make a full investigation of this matter, and in case you ascertain who are the guilty parties, turn them over to the petit juries for punishment. Make the investigation searching and thorough."

davis-davis-1910-08-18.A1:
RACE TROUBLE AT
DAVIS YESTERDAY
FOLLOWING FIGHT BETWEEN NEGRO AND WHITE, NUMBER OF NEGROES LEAVE DAVIS.
Davis, Okla., Aug. 19.—Following his ejectment from the Freeman store yesterday, Asbury Milton, a negro, struck R. Y. Steadman, white, with a brickbat, inflicting a serious wound upon the head. The negro had been ordered out of the store and refusing to go, was forcibly ejected by Mr. Steadman.

Incensed at the negro's action, some of the town's "toughs" made threats against the blacks, which resulted in about 25 of the negroes leaving last night, most of them going to Ardmore. A few others will probably leave today, but the business men of the town today assured the negroes of their safety and no further trouble is expected. Davis' negro population numbers about 75.
davis-davis-1910-08-18.A2:
Negroes Run Out of Davis.
Oklahoma City Aug. 20.—Every negro was driven from the town of Davis, Okla., Friday night and Saturday morning. The whites became enraged over an assault made on R. Y. Steadman, a leading citizen, by a negro, Melton Asberry. Steadman ordered Asberry out of his place of business, whereupon the negro hurled a brick at Steadman, inflicting painful injuries.

tom-hays-andalusia-1910-08-24.A1:
NEGRO RUSHED TO COUNTY JAIL Charged With Murder of Watchmen. COVINGTON CITIZENS ANGERED Deputy Hastens With Prisoner to Montgomery. IN AUTOMOBILE HE RUSHES TO GANTT, WHERE HE TAKES TRAIN FOR CAPITAL CITY WITH PRISONER.
Andalusia, July 31.—(Special.)—Followed by an ever increasing crowd of anygry men, Deputy Sheriff J. M. Johnson raced in an automobile to the railroad station at Gantt, nine miles from this place, with Tom Hayes, a negro accused of the murder of Night Watchman Sowell of the Empire Lumber Company. The killing took place early Sunday morning, but the body was not discovered until late this morning when the day watchman of the place came on duty.

The body was found with a knife stuck in the throat of the victim, and the ground showed that Sowell had fought for a long time before being overcome. The negro was found at his home by Sheriff Presswood, and offered no resistance to arrest.

Upon the discovery of the body of Sowell, the mill operatives became enraged. The knife was thought to belong to the negro Hayes, and the crowd started after him. Sheriff Presswood was ahead of the crowd, and it was only through the use of the automobile that he was able to keep his prisoner from the hands of the crowd which seemed bent upon lynching.

The country surrounding Andalusia is much excited, and Sheriff Presswood thought it best to keep the negro in the Montgomery County jail until his trial.

Sowell was a young man about thirty-five years old, and bore a good reputation. Hayes is said to have been charged on two occasions with violations of the liquor laws of the state, and had been discharged some time ago from the employ of the Empire Lumber Company. The motive of the killing is not known.

Deputy Sheriff Johnson with his prisoner arrived in Montgomery shortly after 7 o'clock Sunday night. At the jail Hayes was asked why he killed Sowell, and the negro replied that he did not kill him. He would not talk of the affair.

NEGROES ARE SHOT DOWN

TEXAS SHERIFF TELLS STORY OF CARNAGE.

Declares Members of Mob Were Filled With Lust for Blood and Shot Down Negroes Indiscriminately.

Palestine, Tex., July 31.—At least fifteen, and it may be twenty, negroes, all of them probably unarmed, were hunted down and killed by a mob numbering perhaps 200 or 300 men, in the Slocum and Denison Springs neighborhood of Palestine last night and yesterday, according to the opinion of Sheriff Black, expressed today.

The sheriff returned early this morning after a twenty-four-hour absence in that district, where racial trouble has been acute, and described in some detail the conditions which he found to exist there. He told of a fierce man hunt in the woods, of riddled bodies found on lonely roads, and of the terror almost indescribable among the inhabitants in the Southeastern part of Anderson County. Sheriff Black is sure that his estimate of the dead is conservative. He said he had made a careful investigation and after telling of its results, added this statement:

"We won't find some of the bodies until the location is revealed to us by the buzzards.

"I found the greatest excitement prevailing throughout that section of the country. Men were going about and killing negroes as fast as they could find them, and so far as I have been able to ascertain, without any real cause at all. These negroes had never done anything that I could discover. There was just a hot-headed gang hunting them down and killing them.

"We found eleven dead bodies, but from what I have heard the dead must number fifteen or twenty. We came across four bodies in one house.

"I don't know how many there were in the mob, but I think there must have been two or three hundred. I understand that Mrs. George Scarborough of Closum saw a party of forty or fifty go through her field.

"I am led to believe that the main trouble was due to a controversy over a promissory note. This may not be true, but that is the impression I have at this stage of the investigation. R. Alford, a white man who is a cripple, had gone on a negro's note. The note came due and he got after the negro to renew it, or pay, or something of the kind, and the negro would not do it, and cursed him. The incident caused bad feeling.

Places Dead at Fifteen.

"If reports that I have given to me are to be credited, there must be fifteen or twenty dead, all of them negroes. It will be difficult to find out just how many were killed, because the dead are scattered all over the woods. Some probably will never be found."

Although every possible effort has been made by the Anderson County authorities, Adjutant-General Newton, Captain Rogers and two or more rangers who arrived this morning, besides others, are lending their aid to the work. Palestine tonight has very little definite information about the trouble between the whites and blacks between Anderson and Denison Springs. Sunday has been characterized by the utter absence of anything authoritative from there except the report which Sheriff Black made on his return at an early hour this morning.

Judge H. B. Garner received a telephone message from Elkhart this afternoon, which purports to come from Captain G. R. Fowler, who is at the

head of a force of special officers in that county. This message was to the effect that everything was quiet and that the troops would not be needed. The man who sent the message informed Judge Gardner that it had been given to him by Captain Fowler with instructions to bring it to Elkhart and transmit it to Palestine.

"I have received a message from Grapeland," said Judge Gardner, "stating that a negro had been killed near Priscilla this morning, and that the parties engaged in it were hunting another negro for the purpose of killing him. They thought something ought to be done to stop it. I have been trying to find out something about the situation, but when I got in touch with Priscilla, I could not find the officer there. I did talk with some man there who said there had been several negroes killed, but he did not indicate what had been done today. Perhaps it is a part of the other trouble.

"Although there was nothing definite, I sent down two additional automobiles this evening with District Attorney Harris, Captain Rogers of the rangers and three or four men. The purpose is to ascertain the situation and advise me as soon as possible.

"The trouble is practically at an end. We are now trying to fix the responsibility and apprehend the guilty parties. I have been informed that one white man has been arrested, and that he is to be brought here. The grand jury will commence work tomorrow afternoon at 2 o'clock. The bailiffs I have sent down into that county are summoning practically everybody. This is for the two-fold purpose of getting the people out of the county, that order may be restored and of obtaining from them such evidence as they may be able to give."

Adjutant-General Newton accompanied by Captain Rogers of the rangers, Col. R. H. Beckham, assistant quartermaster in the Adjutant-General's department, and two members of the Texas Rifle team of 1910, who are scheduled to be in the national shoot at Camp Perry, Ohio, arrived in Palestine this morning from Austin.
tom-hays-andalusia-1910-08-24.A6:
TAKE NEGRO TO DANGER ZONE TOM HAYES RETURNED TO ANDA- LUSIA, WHERE IT IS VERY PROB- ABLE HE WILL BE LYNCHED. By Associated Press.
Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 22.—When officers took Tom Hayes, a negro, back to Andalusia today he was ushered into a danger zone that holds not more than half a chance for him to escape mob wrath. Hayes confesses that he killed a white man at a saw mill.

Holding his victim's head under his left arm, he cut his throat with his right, leaving the knife imbedded in the flesh of his neck where it was found. When he washed his undershirt in the jail after being rushed here at the time of the tragedy to save him from lynching, blood covered the bottom of a big tub.

FLORIDA RAILROAD IS INCORPORATED IN ALABAMA

By Associated Press.

Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 22.—The incorporation of the Alabama, Florida & Southern railroad to run twenty-five miles from Marmill, Ala., to Malone, Fla., is today reported to the secretary of state. The capital is $40,000, all paid in.
tom-hays-andalusia-1910-08-24.A7:
SHERIFF FOILS PLANS OF MOB Brings Prisoner to Montgomery County Jail. MEN ANGERED BY MURDER Troops Called to Protect Prison at Andalusia. SCOUTING PARTY FROM MOB ARRIVES AT JAIL, BUT FACES LINE OF STEEL NEGRO RUSHED AWAY.
Fearing that another attempt to lynch Tom Hayes, a negro, accused of the murder of Night Watchman R. D. Sowell, at the Empire Lumber Company's yard near Andalusia several weeks ago would be made, Sheriff Prestwood of Andalusia Thursday brought Hayes to the Montgomery county jail for safe keeping, following an attempt by a mob of 250 men Wednesday night to lynch the negro.

Upon the discovery that Sowell had been murdered, Hayes was arrested and placed in jail at Andalusia. Shortly after he was locked up, Sheriff Prestwood received word that an attempt would be made to lynch the prisoner and he was brought here for safe keeping. While here, he is said to have confessed to the brutal murder of Sowell. He is said to have admitted that he held his victim's head under one arm, using his free arm to rip the white man's throat.

Several days ago he was taken back to Andalusia as it was thought feeling against him there had died down. This proved not to be the case, however, as on Tuesday night, the night after Hayes was taken back to Andalusia, Sheriff Prestwood says he had information that a mob was going to attempt to storm the jail and lynch Hayes. Sheriff Prestwood notified the commanding officer of the local militia company of what he had heard and the soldiers were held in readiness to protect the jail at a moment's notice. Nothing happened Tuesday night, however, and the militia disbanded.

Wednesday night Sheriff Prestwood was informed that a mob of 250 men had organized several miles from town and was to storm the jail at 2 o'clock Thursday morning. After ascertaining that the mob really intended to storm the jail, Sheriff Prestwood ordered out the militia company and the jail was surrounded by a strong body of soldiers. Several hours later about twenty-five or thirty members of the mob came to Andalusia, evidently to reconnoiter. Upon finding the jail protected, they immediately left the city and nothing more was heard from the mob.

Hayes was brought here on the first train leaving Andalusia and probably will be kept here until his trial is held.
tom-hays-andalusia-1910-08-24.A8:
TOM HAYS TAKEN BACK TO MONTGOMERY AFTER NARROW ESCAPE FROM LYNCHING AT ANDALUSIA. By Associated Press. Montgomery, Ala., Aug. 25.—Tom Hays, taken from here to Andalusia this week to stand trial for the brutal murder of R. D. Sowell, night watchman at a mill, escaped lynching last night only because of the jail being guarded by soldiers. Sheriff Prestwood discovered about 2 a. m. that a mob was forming a few miles out and called the local company into service. When the advance guard of the mob, 25 strong, arrived on a scouting trip, they found the prison too well protected. This morning Sheriff Prestwood rushed the negro back to the Montogmery jail.

tom-hays-andalusia-1910-08-24.A9:
NEGRO NARROWLY
ESCAPES VIOLENCE
Accused Murderer Is Spirited Away From Andalusia
FARMERS ARE THRIFTY
h Wilkinson Issues Annual Bulletin on Fertilizers—Pinchot and Garfeld May Come to Help the Pro-gressive Republicans
Montgomery, August 25.—(Special.) Tom Hayes, accused negro murderer, who barely escaped a mob at Andalusia last night, was glad to get back to the Montgomery county jail today. He was rushed in on the first train out of Andalusia this morning and resumed his old place among the bad boarders of Sheriff Horace Hood with a sigh of relief. Only the watchfulness of the sheriff prevented a mob from getting him, augmented by the presence of soldiers called out on the certainty of danger.

Hayes killed a white man named Sowell, night watchman at a sawmill. From the reports and an alleged confession of the negro himself it appears that he caught the man off his guard at night and grabbed him from behind, throwing his left arm about his head. While his victim was thus held the negro ripped his throat up with a long knife, leaving the weapon sticking in the flesh of the neck. Another story has it that the negro held the pistol of the white man in pawn and that he knew the latter was unarmed.

Talking of the trouble last night Sheriff Prestwood stated that he feared a mob and was on the lookout. About 2 p. m. he was told that a few miles out a mob was forming. He sent out runners who found it to be so. The local military company was at once called out as a consequence. Shortly after they became the jail guard about 25 men, advance of the mob, rode up, but seeing the protection to the prisoner returned and no more was seen or heard of any mob. However, the feeling is high and if the negro is taken back he will likely be killed.
